title: The Handshake in a Post-Handshake World
hook: The pandemic broke the handshake's monopoly, and now many meetings begin with a small negotiation over whether to touch at all.
why:
For most of the last century, the handshake was the default greeting of working life in much of the world. You shook hands at an interview, at the start of a meeting, on closing a deal and at a funeral. Men were taught to do it firmly, look the other man in the eye and never offer a limp hand. Few greetings carried more weight or more advice.

Then, in 2020, it stopped almost overnight. When it returned, it returned as an option rather than a rule. Some people now reach for a hand without thinking, others hold back, and many hesitate for half a second to see what the other person will do. The chapter on male greetings in Part III dealt with how men read and match each other's offers. This chapter looks at the handshake at work: what the research says it does, what a good one involves, why interviews care about it, what the germ evidence shows, how the pandemic changed it, and how to offer, accept or decline one gracefully when you cannot be sure what the other person wants.

teach.p:
It is easy to dismiss the handshake as an empty ritual, but there is evidence that it shapes how an encounter is judged. In a 2012 study, Sanda Dolcos, Florin Dolcos and their colleagues showed people short animated scenes of a host greeting a visitor in an office. In half of the scenes the two shook hands before talking; in the rest they did not. The people watching rated the encounters that began with a handshake more positively, and a handshake softened the bad impression left when one of the figures behaved in a cold or avoidant way.

The researchers also scanned the brains of the people watching. A region involved in processing reward was more active when the scene began with a handshake. That does not mean a handshake is a drug. It does suggest that people treat a handshake as a signal of good intent, and that the signal colours how everything after it is read.

There are limits to what this shows. These were observers watching cartoons, not people shaking hands themselves, and the study did not test whether a handshake changes the outcome of a real meeting. But it fits with ordinary experience: an encounter that opens with a warm, mutual greeting feels like it has started on the right foot, and one that opens with an awkward refusal or a missed hand feels slightly off, however friendly the conversation that follows.

The figures here shake hands in profile, at arm's length, meeting midway. Neither has reached across the other's space. The greeting took two seconds, and it has already told each of them something about the other.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if encounters that began with a handshake were judged no differently from those that did not. In this study they were judged more positively, though the participants were observers rather than the people shaking hands.

teach.p:
The most familiar advice about handshakes is to make them firm. In 2000 William Chaplin and his colleagues put that advice to a test. Four trained coders, two men and two women, each shook hands twice with 112 people and rated the handshakes on several features: the strength of the grip, its vigour, its duration, how completely the hands met, and whether the person made eye contact. The people being greeted also completed personality questionnaires.

The handshakes turned out to be consistent: the same person tended to shake hands in the same way on different occasions and with different coders. A firm handshake, in the full sense of a complete grip, some vigour, a reasonable duration and eye contact, went with more favourable first impressions. It also went with being more extraverted and expressive, and less shy and anxious.

Men's handshakes were firmer on average, but women with firm handshakes made favourable impressions too, and the authors noted that they did not seem to pay the price women often pay for behaving assertively. A later study by Frank Bernieri and Kristen Petty suggested that shaking hands may help men judge one trait more accurately: how conscientious the other person is.

Notice what firm does not mean. It does not mean crushing. The coders were rating a complete, confident grip, not raw pressure. The figure here offers an open, ready posture. A good handshake is an extension of that: the whole hand, a grip that matches the other person's, two or three seconds, and a look at their face.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if handshake quality were unrelated to first impressions. In Chaplin's study, a complete, confident grip with eye contact went with more favourable impressions, though the links to personality were modest and later work has qualified them.
teach.pullQuote: Firm means complete, not crushing: the whole hand, a matched grip, a few seconds and a look at the other person's face.

teach.p:
Job interviews are where handshake advice is most anxious and most insistent. In 2008 Greg Stewart and his colleagues ran mock interviews with 98 students. Trained raters scored each student's handshake, and interviewers made recommendations about whether to hire. Students with better handshakes received more favourable hiring recommendations, even after the researchers accounted for physical appearance and dress.

The study also suggested why. More extraverted students tended to give better handshakes, and the handshake appeared to carry part of the link between extraversion and the interviewers' judgments. Women's handshakes were rated lower on average, but women were not rated as less suitable, and the link between handshake and rating may have been stronger for them.

It would be easy to draw the wrong lesson. The study does not show that training your grip will get you a job. A handshake is a small, visible sample of social ease, and the people with good handshakes were probably at ease in other ways too: in how they sat, spoke and looked at the interviewer. The handshake may have been one sign of that ease rather than its cause.

The useful lesson is narrower. Interviewers notice the opening seconds, and a handshake that is limp, sweaty or crushing can start things badly. Practise a few times with a friend until a complete, matched grip feels natural, then stop thinking about it. A later chapter on interviews looks at what interviewers can and cannot read, from both sides of the desk. The figure here waits upright before being called in, hands loose rather than wringing.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if handshake quality bore no relation to interview ratings. In Stewart's study it did, even with appearance and dress accounted for, though the handshake may be a sign of social ease rather than a cause of success.

teach.p:
Most bad handshakes fall into a few familiar kinds. The crusher squeezes hard enough to hurt, often as a show of strength, and leaves the other person with the impression of someone who competes where he should connect. The fish is a limp, passive hand that gives nothing back. The fingertip grip catches only the other person's fingers, usually because someone reached too early. The pump goes on shaking for too long. The yank pulls the other person off balance towards you.

There are also handshakes that try to say something about status. Popular books describe turning your hand palm down on top of the other person's as a dominance move, or adding a second hand on their wrist or shoulder to show warmth or control. These ideas are widely repeated but little tested. What is clear is that any handshake that makes the other person feel managed tends to be read as a power play, however it was meant.

For many people the real problem is simpler: anxiety. Hands get cold and damp when you are nervous, and a damp handshake is one of the things people dread most. The practical fixes are unglamorous. Hold any cold drink in your left hand, so your right hand stays dry and warm. Wipe your palm discreetly on a handkerchief or your trousers before you stand. Keep your hands loose and still, not wringing, in the minutes beforehand.

The figure here wrings his hands while waiting, a sign of nerves that also tends to make palms damper. Letting them rest open, or holding something, gives the anxiety less to work with.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if crushing, limp or prolonged handshakes were judged as favourably as complete, matched ones. Chaplin's coders rated the features of a good handshake together, and grips at either extreme rarely make a good impression.
teach.pullQuote: Any handshake that makes the other person feel managed is read as a power play, whatever you meant by it.

teach.p:
Doctors and infection specialists had worried about handshakes long before 2020. Hands carry bacteria and viruses, and a handshake brings two palms into firm, prolonged contact. In 2014 Sara Mela and David Whitworth at Aberystwyth University compared greetings directly. They had people wear sterile gloves, dipped one gloved hand in a harmless strain of bacteria, and measured how much transferred during a handshake, a high five and a fist bump.

The handshake transferred the most. A high five transferred considerably less, and a fist bump far less again. Longer and stronger handshakes transferred more, which makes sense: more contact, for longer, over a larger area. The authors suggested the fist bump as a more hygienic alternative, particularly in hospitals, where staff greet large numbers of people and infection matters most.

The study has limits. It used gloves rather than bare hands, and a single kind of bacteria, so it gives a sense of the relative difference rather than the risk of any particular greeting. Hand washing matters more than any choice of greeting, and Whitworth himself doubted that a no-contact greeting would ever replace the handshake entirely.

But the principle is useful. When you are ill, when the other person is frail or unwell, or when you are in a hospital or care home, the kindest greeting may be the one with the least contact. The figures here bump fists: brief, light and involving only the knuckles. It is informal, and not right for every setting, but it carries some of the warmth of touch at a fraction of the contact.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if a fist bump transferred as many bacteria as a handshake. In Mela and Whitworth's study it transferred far fewer, though the experiment used gloves rather than bare hands.

teach.p:
In April 2020, early in the pandemic, Anthony Fauci, then the leading infectious disease official in the United States, said on a podcast that he did not think people should ever shake hands again. For a while, in many countries, almost nobody did. People improvised: elbow bumps, foot taps, nods, waves, and the hand placed on the heart that many cultures already used.

The handshake did not disappear. In much of the world it returned, but not entirely and not for everyone. Some people dropped it for good, especially those who are older, unwell, caring for someone vulnerable, or simply relieved to have a reason not to touch strangers. Others never stopped. The result is that the handshake is no longer the single expected greeting at work. It is one option among several, and the choice is now often made on the spot, by both people, in the second before they meet.

That second is where things can go wrong. One person's hand comes out while the other's stays down, or two people hesitate at once and neither moves. The awkwardness is small but real, and it falls hardest on the person who offered and was not met.

A useful default is to signal before you touch. As you approach, let your hand begin to come forward, slowly enough that the other person can respond, and watch what they do. If their hand comes out, shake it. If it stays down, turn the movement into a hand on your heart or a small open gesture and nod. The figure here greets with a hand on the heart, a greeting that says you are glad to see someone without asking anything of them.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if almost everyone had returned to shaking hands as automatically as before 2020. Many people did, but many did not, which is why reading the offer has become part of the greeting.

teach.p:
Because the handshake is now a choice, it helps to know how to make that choice well. When you are unsure, let the other person lead. A host, an older person or someone more senior often sets the greeting, and matching their choice is rarely wrong. If you offer a hand and it is not taken, withdraw it without fuss, smile and say something warm. The person who declined was probably not rejecting you.

Some people do not shake hands for reasons of faith. Many observant Muslims and Orthodox Jews do not shake hands with someone of the opposite sex outside their close family, and may offer a hand on the heart or a nod instead. In parts of Asia a bow, a wai or palms pressed together may be the expected greeting. Others decline because of health, disability, pain in their hands or a history that makes touch from strangers unwelcome. You do not need to know the reason. You only need to accept the choice gracefully.

If you are the one declining, do it warmly and early, before the other person's hand is fully out. Smile, nod, place a hand on your heart or raise it in a small wave, and say something like, I'm not shaking hands at the moment, but it's very good to meet you. The warmth of the words and face does the work the handshake would have done. Most people will take their cue from you and move on in a second.

The figure here greets with palms pressed together, the wai used in Thailand. Greetings like this are complete in themselves. They are not lesser versions of a handshake, and offering one is not a refusal to connect.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if declining a handshake warmly were usually taken as an insult. In practice a clear, friendly alternative offered early is accepted by most people, and the awkward moments come from hesitation rather than refusal.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Stepping in too far for the grip
poseGallery.annotation: A handshake works at arm's length. Closing the gap as you grip turns a greeting into a crowding move.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Wringing hands before being called in
poseGallery.annotation: Wringing feeds the nerves and dampens the palms. Let your hands rest, and keep any cold drink in your left hand.

poseGallery.doCaption: Declining with a hand on the heart
poseGallery.annotation: A refusal with no alternative feels like a rejection. A hand on the heart and a smile says yes to the person while saying no to the touch.

poseGallery.dontCaption: A full handshake on a hospital ward
poseGallery.annotation: Where infection matters, less contact is kinder. A fist bump keeps some warmth at a fraction of the contact.

caseStudy:
Arjun, thirty-four, manages a team at an engineering firm and has always shaken hands with everyone. During the pandemic he stopped, and when restrictions lifted he went straight back to it. For months he did not notice that some people met his hand a little late, or not at all.

Then, at the start of a supplier meeting, he reached out to a woman from the other company. She hesitated, then said, smiling, that she didn't shake hands, and put her hand on her heart. Arjun froze with his hand in the air, said sorry twice, and spent the first ten minutes of the meeting feeling clumsy. Later he realised he had made the moment far more awkward than she had.

He changed his approach. Now, as he walks up to someone, he lets his hand start to come forward slowly and watches. If their hand comes up, he shakes it: whole hand, a matched grip, a couple of seconds. If it does not, he turns the movement into a hand on his chest and a nod, and says it's good to meet them. He has stopped apologising when a hand is not taken.

He also noticed that one of his engineers, Tom, had a crushing grip that made visitors wince, and that Tom's palms were often damp before presentations. Arjun told him, privately and lightly, about both. Tom was embarrassed, but he eased his grip and started carrying his coffee in his left hand.

When Arjun's father went into hospital that winter, Arjun found himself bumping fists with the nurses instead of shaking hands. It felt odd at first. By the end of the week it felt like the most natural greeting there.
observe: Notice the half second before a greeting this week, and who moves first to offer a hand.
Notice how different people respond to an offered hand: matching it, hesitating or offering something else.
Notice your own grip when you shake hands. Is it complete, matched and brief, or does it lean towards crushing or limp?
Notice your hands in the minutes before a stressful meeting, and whether they are cold, damp or busy.

drills.name: Grip Calibration
steps: Ask a friend or partner to shake hands with you five times.
Vary your grip from very light to very firm, and ask them to say which felt best.
Try matching their grip rather than setting your own.
Check that your whole palm meets theirs, not just your fingers.
Practise a two- or three-second shake with a look at their face, then stop.

drills.name: The Slow Offer
steps: For three greetings this week, let your hand start to come forward slowly as you approach.
Watch what the other person's hand does.
If it comes up, shake it. If it stays down, turn the movement into a nod or a hand on your heart.
Note how each greeting felt, and whether any were awkward.

drills.name: A Warm Decline
steps: Write one sentence you could use to decline a handshake warmly, such as I'm not shaking hands at the moment, but it's very good to meet you.
Choose a gesture to go with it: a hand on your heart, a small wave or a nod.
Practise both in a mirror until the gesture comes early, before the other person's hand is fully out.
Rehearse it once with a friend who offers a hand.
Keep the sentence ready for when you are unwell or the other person is vulnerable.

drills.name: Pre-Meeting Hands
steps: Before your next interview or important meeting, notice your hands in the ten minutes beforehand.
If they are wringing or fidgeting, let them rest still and open.
Hold any cold drink in your left hand.
Wipe your right palm discreetly just before you stand.

quiz.q: A colleague insists that a really firm handshake, as strong as you can make it, is what makes a good impression. What does the evidence suggest?
options: He is right; the hardest grips made the best impressions in every study of handshakes
A complete, matched grip with eye contact makes a good impression, while crushing does not
Grip makes no difference at all, because people form impressions only from faces and voices
A limp grip is best, because it shows people that you are gentle and that you mean no harm
quiz.explain: Chaplin's coders rated firmness as a combination of a complete grip, vigour, duration and eye contact. A crushing grip is a different thing, and it is usually read as competition rather than confidence.

quiz.q: What did Stewart and colleagues find in their 2008 study of mock job interviews?
options: Handshakes had no link with hiring recommendations once dress and appearance were controlled
Better handshakes went with better hiring recommendations, even with appearance and dress controlled
Only men's handshakes mattered, because interviewers ignored women's handshakes entirely
Interviewers rated weak handshakes more highly, because they read them as signs of humility
quiz.explain: Students with better handshakes received more favourable recommendations, and the handshake carried part of the link between extraversion and those judgments. It may be a sign of social ease rather than a cause of success.

quiz.q: In Mela and Whitworth's study of greetings and bacteria, which greeting transferred the fewest bacteria?
options: The handshake, as long as the grip was kept firm and short
The high five, because the palms met so very briefly
The fist bump, which involved the smallest area of contact
All three greetings transferred about the same amount of bacteria
quiz.explain: The handshake transferred the most and the fist bump the least, with the high five in between. Longer and stronger handshakes transferred more. The study used gloves, so it shows the relative difference rather than the risk of any one greeting.

quiz.q: You are about to greet a visitor and are not sure whether she shakes hands. What fits this chapter best?
options: Let your hand start forward slowly, then shake or switch to a nod and a smile
Keep your hands down and wait for her to make the first move, however long it takes
Push your hand out quickly and firmly, so that she cannot hesitate or say no
Ask her directly and at length about her views on shaking hands before you start
quiz.explain: A slow offer gives the other person time to respond. If her hand comes up, shake it; if it does not, turning the movement into a nod or a hand on your heart keeps the greeting warm.

quiz.q: A man from another company declines your offered hand and places his hand on his heart instead. What is the most likely meaning?
options: He is signalling dislike and does not want to work with you
He is greeting you warmly in a way that does not involve touch
He is testing whether you will insist on shaking his hand anyway
He has misunderstood and expected you to bow to him first
quiz.explain: A hand on the heart is a complete, warm greeting in many cultures. People decline handshakes for reasons of faith, health or comfort, and the gesture says they are glad to meet you without the touch.

quiz.q: Which conclusion does Dolcos and colleagues' 2012 study of handshakes support?
options: A handshake guarantees that any meeting will have a good outcome
Handshakes matter only when the people involved already know each other
Watching a handshake made no difference to how encounters were judged
Observers judged encounters that began with a handshake more positively
quiz.explain: People watching animated scenes rated encounters that began with a handshake more favourably, and a handshake softened the impact of cold behaviour. The participants were observers, so the study does not show what happens in real meetings.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific greeting at work in the last month that felt awkward: a missed hand, a hesitation, a grip that was too hard or too limp. Describe who moved first, what each of you did with your hands and how the moment ended. What would a slow offer have changed? Then describe how you would decline a handshake warmly if you needed to, and what words and gesture you would use.
reflection.guidance: Awkward greetings are common and usually forgotten quickly, so there is nothing to be embarrassed about. The point is to notice your own habits: whether you reach too fast, grip too hard, or freeze when a hand is not met. Be specific about the moment, including where you were standing and what was said.

failureMode: The first failure is to treat firm as meaning hard, and to crush hands as a show of strength. The second is to push a hand out quickly and expect it to be taken, leaving the other person to refuse an offer they never wanted. The third is to take a declined handshake as an insult, when the reason is usually faith, health or comfort. The fourth is to make the moment worse with repeated apologies, when a smile and a warm word would let it pass. The fifth is to put a full handshake on someone who is ill, frail or in hospital, when a lighter greeting would be kinder. And the sixth is to believe a perfect grip will win an interview, when it is at most one small sign of being at ease.
